title: The distinction between the natural and spiritual mind
english: …discover by reasoning what has been revealed to us; we also proclaim it. We do not dress it up in fine words but "compare spiritual things with spiritual," grasping his revelations by the power of the Spirit and proclaiming them in due order. "Comparing spiritual things with spiritual": when a second revelation interprets and clarifies the earlier one, those who received the revelations compared the later with the earlier, found them the same, and so gained a firmer assurance of the truth revealed.

The second catena form adds: Of a man he said "the spirit that is in him," but of the Holy Spirit he did not say "that is in God"; he said "that is from God." There is a great difference between "in him" and "from God." He was exact when he called the Holy Spirit "from God," as a living being with its own subsistence, and the unclean spirit "of the world," as something that fills out the world's substance; for the devil is part of its creation, in that he came into being. The word "comparing" can also be taken in the opposite sense, as "distinguishing" and "separating"; but the first sense is better.

On 1 Corinthians 2:14–15: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit." By "natural" he means the man who keeps in step with his own reasonings. "For they are folly to him." So deep is the spiritual revelation that to the wise of this world it looks like folly, so far beyond their grasp is God's revelation. The grace of the Holy Spirit, as it displayed its power, refuted the man of technique, and not by technique but by the force of its wonders. Spiritual people do not overturn reasonings with reasonings. They receive the mind that comes from God and the revelation that comes from there, and they speak from that, so that whoever opposes them is not refuting reasonings but setting himself against the knowledge of God. That is why he says, "For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, his knowledge.

The second catena form adds: Or he means the man who is sick in the reasonings of his soul and is not sound in his grasp of the truth, just as he calls "fleshly" the man who is sick with fleshly desires and a slave of pleasures. So the natural man cannot take the truth in. His soul has been so damaged that he thinks God's dispensation and grace are folly. "And he cannot know, because he is examined spiritually." The natural man looks for clever arguments about the cross and pushes the preaching away as foolish and unconvincing. Because he does not look to the wonders the Spirit works, he can no longer even see that he is setting himself against the truth while the power and wonders of the Spirit refute him. "Is examined" means that he is refuted closely and after scrutiny. But the spiritual man, who has received the Spirit, uses the signs he displays to refute everything that others wrongly bring as refutation, while he himself is refuted by no one.
